headline: The shrinking number of prosecutors bringing DOJ’s high-profile cases
author: Perry Stein

paragraphs.text: Earlier this year, Alessandra Serano, a trusted aide to Attorney General Todd Blanche, flew to South Florida to help prosecutors investigating President Donald Trump’s political foes. Serano, the Justice Department’s first-ever coordinator for child exploitation and human trafficking, zipped back to D.C. last month to ask a judge to sign off on a warrant to search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar (D).

Stanley Woodward, the third-highest ranking official at the Justice Department, recently put his signature on court filings about Trump’s White House ballroom project, a pre-election lawsuit seeking to potentially block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska and a call for an antitrust investigation into major TV networks that suspended their pooled coverage of the president.
And when the Justice Department charged former FBI director James B. Comey for the third time last month, two close aides to Blanche signed off on the court documents.
As Donald Trump enters his final years in office, the Justice Department is relying on a shrinking number of lawyers to bring the department’s most high-profile and controversial cases.

That marks a sharp change from how the Justice Department operated under previous administrations, during which political appointees rarely waded into courtrooms and instead left the litigating, even in fraught cases, to rank-and-file career prosecutors.

The strategy under Blanche has wound up insulating career staffers from the most controversial cases, enabling them to focus on more traditional Justice Department matters without getting drawn into politically fraught investigations. That also means fewer career prosecutors are at risk of quitting over case assignments they feel could imperil their legal ethics, which was a frequent occurrence during the first year of the Trump administration.

But, according to former Justice Department officials, the reliance on political appointees and what are known as special assistant U.S. attorneys has further eroded trust in the agency and federal law enforcement. Special assistant U.S. attorneys are typically career lawyers already working in the government who are either detailed or appointed to work on a specific case.

This article is based on interviews with current and former Justice Department officials, some of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to freely discuss their observations of the current administration.

During Trump’s second term, he has repeatedly called for his foes to face investigations and charges, and Justice Department leaders have seemed eager to oblige him. But critics say assigning people viewed as being tied to political appointees to these cases suggests the Trump administration is wielding the law enforcement agency to benefit the president and his allies.

“Cases originate from the ground, not the top,” said Kyle Boynton, a former career civil rights prosecutor who left the department last year. “In this administration, they have been originating from the top. It is such a sharp departure from the expectations that Americans should have of how law enforcement works in this country.”
“That’s why we call it building a case,” he said. “You don’t build a case down from the clouds; you build a foundation first.”

The Justice Department, in a statement, said it was not heavily relying on political appointees to bring these notable cases and that assignments are based on expertise and resources. The agency also said it was taking a “more dynamic approach than previous administrations.”

“To compare Departments across administrations is not an apples-to-apples comparison, as the Biden administration’s approach and priorities created a unique climate coming into 2025,” a spokesperson for the agency said.

The spokesperson said these high-profile matters, including the Florida grand conspiracy investigation and the Omar probe, are not its biggest cases, pointing instead to major fraud and trafficking investigations, which career and political appointees work on together.

Still, Blanche’s approach has coincided with the Justice Department being hollowed out by an exodus of career staffers, most of whom resigned amid upheaval in the agency under Trump or were fired over their reluctance to work on certain cases.

U.S. attorney offices across the country are stretched thin, with some unable to keep up with the mounting workload, which includes an uptick in immigration cases, according to current and former officials.
The Justice Department has defended its staffing decisions, citing declining violent crime rates across the country and saying that it is prosecuting criminals in high numbers.

“The Department is doing more with a leaner workforce because it has stopped funding bloated bureaucracy and activist work outside its core mission,” a department spokesperson said in a statement. “Those who want a Justice Department focused on politics instead of public safety should never again be trusted with the safety of the American people.”

Blanche, a former federal prosecutor who later served as Trump’s defense attorney, understands the role of line prosecutors and wants them to keep doing the day-to-day work of investigating and charging strong cases, according to two people familiar with his thinking who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private conversations.

His decision to assign the department’s most controversial cases to the prosecutors who want to work on them, and who are often political appointees or close to him, has enabled other attorneys to conduct their cases with fewer disturbances, former agency officials said.

But the prosecutors tasked with bringing these fraught cases often have far less experience or skill litigating them than many of the veteran career attorneys who work under them, former Justice Department officials noted.

The former officials said that comparative lack of experience and skill shows, pointing out that the biggest political cases brought by this administration have faltered after they were rejected by grand juries, dismissed by judges or stalled in the investigatory stages. Legal experts said the department’s struggles in court are also a reflection of the sometimes weak cases prosecutors are bringing in these matters.
As Blanche prepares for the second half of Trump’s second term, none of the Justice Department’s defining cases against Trump’s political foes have gone to trial.

Cases against Comey, New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) and two former FBI officials who were accused of making false statements about their knowledge of a laptop belonging to Hunter Biden have all been dismissed by judges. The Justice Department is seeking to revive the cases against Comey and James. Another case against Comey could go to trial sometime next year.

Historically, grand juries rarely decline to approve indictments sought by prosecutors. But during Trump’s second term, such panels have rejected indictments in high-profile instances, including attempts to bring charges against six Democratic lawmakers, former Trump aide Cassidy Hutchinson and people accused of voter fraud.

In Florida, the “grand conspiracy” case — which is examining whether Obama- and Biden-era officials violated Trump’s rights as they investigated him — has yielded no indictments and appears to be faltering.

That investigation is being run out of the U.S. attorney’s office in South Florida, though the Justice Department has kept it separate from the day-to-day operations there, staffing it with political appointees and prosecutors across the country, many of whom volunteered to work on the probe.
The Justice Department in recent weeks dispatched the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles to Florida to work on that investigation.

The prosecutor, Bill Essayli — one of the Justice Department’s most vocal backers of Trump — is a former Republican state politician who has been at the forefront of the administration’s efforts to investigate non citizens accused of voter fraud and prosecute protesters who allegedly impeded immigration officials from doing their jobs.

This new assignment means that Essayli is running one of the biggest U.S. attorney’s office, where he has to oversee hundreds of prosecutors and thousands of cases, while also working as a prosecutor on an investigation on a different coast.
Blanche’s strategy for which officials handle high-profile efforts has also drawn praise.

Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney in the Southern District of Texas, said these cases represent a sliver of the Justice Department’s caseload. Reitz said it makes sense Blanche would want his most trusted allies to handle these sensitive matters while allowing the thousands of career prosecutors to focus on their work.
“Todd is a firm believer that the overwhelming majority of the work that we do is bipartisan, nonpartisan, bread-and-butter law enforcement work,” Reitz said in an interview.

“But like any other administration, there are special projects that arise that involve a special degree of sensitivity that have to be entrusted to certain people,” said Reitz, a conservative prosecutor who has threatened to investigate Democrats over their scrutiny of Trump.

In the first year of the Trump administration, prosecutors and other lawyers have quit the Justice Department after being asked to take actions or work on cases they felt compromised their ethics, The Washington Post has previously reported.

The Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section — tasked with investigating and prosecuting public officials — was gutted when many prosecutors refused to sign off on dropping a case against then-New York Mayor Eric Adams (D). Federal prosecutors in New York were also pushed out or quit because of the administration’s desire to drop the case.

In Virginia, at least a half-dozen prosecutors were demoted or pushed out due to fallout from the push to prosecute Comey. In Tennessee, a top prosecutor resigned in protest over the controversial indictment of a Maryland man who had successfully challenged his illegal deportation to El Salvador.

Since the beginning of the administration, more than 7,000 of the agency’s 20,000 or so staffers — a roster that includes lawyers and nonlawyers alike — who work at Justice Department headquarters and U.S. attorney’s offices across the country have left, according to Justice Connection, an advocacy organization founded by former employees. In their place, 3,500 people have been hired, Justice Connection found.
The Justice Department said in response to questions for this article that it has hired more than 1,100 assistant U.S. attorneys, who are the prosecutors who work across the country.

Reitz said when he was installed in July as the U.S. attorney in South Texas, overseeing an office that stretches from Houston to the U.S.-Mexico border, there was a 35 percent vacancy rate in staffing.
The prosecutor said he has chipped away at the vacancy rate, bringing it down to about 25 percent. He achieved that, he said, through $20,000 signing bonuses and relocation stipends.

“We are accomplishing our mission even with a leaner staff, but it is of course true that we can do more with more people,” Reitz said. “I’m not experiencing heartburn yet over declining cases because we don’t have staff.”
Some offices are experiencing that anxiety. People interviewed for this article said departed prosecutors have had to hand off their open cases to remaining staff, leaving whole offices backlogged.
Department leaders are also struggling to address litigation around an unprecedented number of immigration arrests.

Charles Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney in the Western District of Washington, wrote in an unusual letter to a federal judge this month that his office did not have staff to defend every “habeas corpus” case mounted by someone challenging their detention.

In these cases, immigrants write petitions to the courts saying that federal officials are unlawfully detaining them. Typically, prosecutors would defend the government, explaining to a judge why the people were rightfully detained.

But Floyd wrote to the judge that such a defense was not possible anymore, saying that “to conserve resources, there will be many habeas cases in which” his office would “no longer assume responsibility for providing a defense.”
Floyd later said his office would again assign staff members to these cases.
Blanche acknowledged in a memo this month that the increase in immigration arrests, and a flood of people challenging their detention, has strained U.S. attorney offices.
The attorney general said he was surging resources in response, requiring attorneys from across the department, including antitrust and civil rights attorneys, to pitch in.
